newsitem.title: USA: Welfare reform threatens Calif counties - controller.
newsitem.headline: Welfare reform threatens Calif counties - controller.

text.p: California state Controller Kathleen Connell warned Tuesday that welfare reform could undermine local government finances and could even bankrupt counties already in fiscal trouble.

"If a sufficient number of welfare recipients are not moved into jobs, county governments could be forced to add thousands of people to their general assistance rolls," Connell said. "This could potentially bankrupt counties already on the fiscal edge."
Connell issued her warning in a report by the state's Work Opportunity Response Commission.
The commission was formed in October to help lawmakers implement the jobs component of federal welfare reform.
Under the new reforms, several public assistance programs are affected, most notably Aid to Families with Dependent Children, which has been eliminated.

In its place, states will receive block grants that set new conditions on aid. Able-bodied recipients will no longer be entitled to receive cash payments for more than five years, and assistance will be discontinued if they do not engage in work activities within two years. States that fail to meet the welfare-to-work targets risk reductions in their block grants.
"I believe this is the single most important fiscal challenge facing our state as we enter the next century," Connell said in the commission's report.

To help ease the effect of welfare reforms, the report included recommended, among other things, that California should offer a state-level welfare-to-work tax credit to businesses employing welfare recipients.

The state-level credit should be equal to one-third of the federal tax credit, the commission said. The federal tax credit recently proposed by President Clinton would provide employers a 50 percent tax credit on the first $10,000 in wages earned by a long-term welfare recipient.

The California commission said the federal tax credit program should be expanded to allow companies to elect to receive a federal refund of 50 percent of the credit amount, or allow the companies to carryback and carryforward the full amount of the tax credit.
The commission said the state welfare-to-work tax credit should be tied to the federal program. It said the state and federal eligibility requirements should be the same.
The commission also recommended the state set baseline targets that counties must meet for moving recipients off the welfare rolls with adjustments for local conditions.
The Work Opportunity Response Commission's recommendations were presented to Gov. Pete Wilson, the state Legislature as well as to Clinton.
